as_told: In 1975 Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built the first digital camera. Kodak's managers feared it would kill their film business, so they buried it and hid it away. Rivals later took the digital market, and Kodak went bankrupt in 2012.
lesson: Incumbent companies fail because they suppress new technology that threatens their existing business.
what_happened: Steven Sasson built a portable electronic still camera at Kodak in 1975; it recorded images digitally on a cassette tape and played them back on a TV. Kodak filed a patent on it on 20 May 1977, naming Gareth A. Lloyd and Sasson as inventors, and the patent was published on 26 December 1978, so the invention was public. Sasson wrote in 2007 that he showed it to many internal Kodak audiences in 1976, that they asked sceptical questions, that he expected 15 to 20 years before it could reach consumers, and that apart from the patent the work was not shown publicly until 2001. Kodak did not make that prototype into a product, but by its own account it made the first megapixel CCD image sensor in 1986, introduced a professional digital camera system for photojournalists in 1991 and launched the DC40 consumer digital camera in 1995.
false_part: Kodak did not bury the invention: it patented it publicly in 1978, kept developing digital imaging and sold digital cameras from 1991.

lesson_verdict.why: Experts surveyed on the 77 cases that Christensen's work offers as disruptive innovation, Kodak among them, found that only seven fit all four key parts of the theory. So Kodak's fall does not by itself show that incumbents fail because they suppress threatening technology.

source.what: King, A. A. and Baatartogtokh, B. (2015), 'How useful is the theory of disruptive innovation?', MIT Sloan Management Review 57(1)
source.quote: only seven of the cases (9%) exhibited all four elements of the theory

confidence_note: The 1986, 1991 and 1995 dates come from Kodak's own website, not from records made at the time. The often-quoted line that managers said 'that's cute, but don't tell anyone about it' is Sasson's account relayed by reporters (New York Times 2008, 2015); in his own 2007 post he describes sceptical questions, not an order to hide it. What is false is that the invention was buried: it was patented in public in 1978, and Kodak sold digital cameras from 1991.
